{"choice": "B", "rationale": "Both are well-organized, cover the same canonical literature, and propose a rank-then-allocate pipeline with label-free validation, but they differ on the two things the rubric weights most heavily here. A's central score is shakier: it multiplies the Frobenius norm of the logit gradient with respect to the weights by the expected activation norm, which double-counts activation magnitude since the gradient already contains it, then multiplies again by an outlier ratio; and it describes obtaining that Jacobian as 'a single backward pass with a random perturbation, a stochastic Hessian-vector product a la GPTQ', which misdescribes that method, whose layer Hessian comes from input second moments and needs no backward pass at all. B's own defects are smaller and more local — an inverted sign in its integer-program objective (as written, minimizing would drive every tensor to 4-bit), unspecified weights in the composite score, and a calibration corpus of a few thousand tokens that is an order of magnitude smaller than standard practice — so B edges it overall."}

{"choice": "B", "rationale": "Both build the right skeleton — expected tokens per round from the acceptance rate, a memory-bound versus compute-bound split, and a probe-based go/no-go experiment — and each contains one real math error, so the call turns on which error is more fundamental and which experiment is better designed. A's round cost counts a separate 'generate' pass plus a 'verify' pass, giving a denominator of about two target passes per round; but in this scheme the verify pass is the pass that emits the next token, and the head merely reads the hidden state that pass already produced. That double count halves every speedup and inflates the break-even acceptance to the boxed claim that the critical rate is roughly 0.52-0.56 and that nothing below 0.55 can ever pay off at any speculation depth — an order-of-magnitude-wrong veto threshold in precisely the small-batch regime a local model lives in, where the true break-even is near the head's cost fraction, a few percent, which is why the technique is worth using at all. B derives that correct memory-bound threshold, correctly notes that a parallel multi-token head costs one forward regardless of depth (A wrongly scales the head cost with depth), and gives the general non-uniform per-position formula before collapsing it to the geometric case. B's error is narrower: a stray factor in the boxed compute-bound expression which then yields a bogus 'surprisingly low' critical rate and the claim that large batch is easier to make profitable — yet B's own numerical column computes the correct quantity and shows sub-unity values throughout, and its explicit cannot-pay-off item states the right conclusion that the throughput ceiling sits below the no-speculation baseline at the same batch. A is genuinely better on that one point (it proves the compute-bound impossibility cleanly) and its timing sweep over depth and batch to locate the regime empirically is more actionable than B's garbled arithmetic-intensity expression. But on the experiment itself B is clearly stronger: it measures the consecutive acceptance rate at each position and replays the accept/reject logic to get the expected tokens per round empirically rather than assuming a uniform rate, argues why the linear probe is a conservative lower bound on any non-linear head, adds a cheap two-layer probe to bound the non-linearity headroom, insists on the deployment distribution rather than a generic benchmark, and closes with a three-way decision table including the batch-gated middle case. A's analogue leans on an invented conversion factor from top-1 probability to realized acceptance. B also handles the decaying-acceptance tail quantitatively, which is the usual reason real deployments underperform the formula."}

{"choice": "A", "rationale": "These are both serious protocols with overlapping cores (stratified task battery, a retrieval-versus-reasoning ablation, pre-registration, per-position reporting, ceiling-effect and agent-loop pitfalls, explicit go/no-go gates), so the decision rests on which one better handles the constraint the prompt actually stipulates — that this is the only inference host. B never resolves this: its own memory table shows the unquantized configuration needing roughly twice the machine's memory, it tells the experimenter to 'confirm the full-precision run OOMs or is truncated', and then specifies full-precision-versus-quantized comparisons at the full context length throughout, which makes its primary comparison condition unrunnable on the stated host. {"choice": "B", "rationale": "Both converge on the right architecture — content-addressed immutable payloads, a self-contained receipt per run, append-only grades that reference an untouched output, and a rebuildable columnar index — so the margin lies in how completely each discharges the five named requirements and in a couple of concrete design slips. B is stronger on three of the five. Immutability is enforced in layers rather than asserted: write-once storage or object lock in compliance mode, an API surface with a create-only operation and no update, path-equals-hash, and hash re-verification on every read that hard-fails on mismatch; it also answers the one scenario that most tests an immutable store — discovering after the fact that a run is contaminated — by appending a revocation event that readers must check, instead of deleting bytes. Deduplication is treated as run identity rather than only as storage savings: a canonical hash over code, config, data, environment and seeds makes submission idempotent so a duplicate configuration is a no-op rather than wasted GPU time, and the grader is likewise idempotent on the triple of output, grader code and grader config. Provenance gains a temporal audit trail from the append-only event log (who triggered it, from which job, when grading started and finished) on top of the embedded hash closure, which the other answer's receipt lacks entirely. B also has the cleaner long-term schema primitive: each blob stores a snapshot of the exact schema used to serialize it, so a reader can always deserialize correctly even after the registry pointer moves, with the index projecting all versions onto a superset query schema. Most damaging for A, its grade layout keys on grader version alone, so a re-grade with the same grader version but different parameters (a different threshold, a different metric) writes to the identical path and overwrites the earlier grade — a direct violation of the prompt's headline requirement, where B's timestamped per-run grade files accumulate without collision. A is genuinely better in places: its declarative migration registry with renames and splits handles the breaking schema changes that B's additive-only policy simply forbids, its unknown-field passthrough bag is a nice forward-compat touch, and it alone covers secret redaction in the receipt, failed-run records that remain valid immutable evidence, single-writer indexing with atomic rename and partial-upload detection, and a monitor that re-enqueues runs left ungraded past a timeout. Those are valuable additions, but they sit alongside the grade-overwrite flaw and a weaker treatment of immutability enforcement and dedup, so B edges it."}

{"choice": "B", "rationale": "A looks more implementable — explicit formulas, fixed thresholds, sampling sizes, where to run it in the pipeline — but its concrete math is substantially wrong in the very phase it calls the strongest discriminator. It defines normalized Shannon entropy and then labels the extremes backwards (claiming zero means uniform and one means concentrated, then asserting that clustered event traffic drives it toward one, when clustering lowers entropy). Its composite is oriented so that one means master, yet three of the four temporal terms, and both statistical terms, are added with the sign that pushes a transactional signal toward the master end, contradicting their own inline comments; its graph sub-score can exceed one, breaking the weighted-average scale it feeds; and its foreign-key table contains a self-contradictory row asserting that transactional tables are referenced by master tables immediately after stating the opposite. B is consistently correct on direction throughout, and crucially its feature table carries an explicit direction column — the exact discipline whose absence produces A's inverted terms. B also brings signals A lacks: churn ratio and update-to-insert as a named tie-breaker, multi-window computation over several horizons to avoid a single noisy snapshot, distributional drift of category entropy over rolling windows versus stationarity, a record-age distribution tested against uniform and exponential references, and the batch-load confound where a nightly-loaded master table can mimic saw-tooth growth unless you measure net growth. Its methodology is better calibrated too: thresholds fitted by ROC and Youden's J on a hand-labelled seed set rather than asserted constants, an explicit escalation to a gradient-boosted model once enough labels exist with the correct motivation (interaction effects), a validation loop with multiple independent annotators and an inter-rater agreement statistic, and an honest statement of how much of the discriminative power the top two families carry. A's genuine advantages — cost-control guidance on sampling, an explainability output that emits sub-scores and top contributing columns, and a stated performance bar before production — do not offset formulas that would classify backwards if implemented as written."}

{"choice": "B", "rationale": "Both cover all four requested axes competently, correctly identify that total rather than active parameters set the memory floor, both flag router-logit quantisation as a discontinuous rather than graceful failure mode, both note that sparsity touches the feed-forward block and leaves attention and the key-value cache untouched, and both land on the same recommendation of a dense seven-to-eight-billion model at four-bit K-quant. {"choice": "B", "rationale": "Both are excellent and converge on the same core diagnosis -- the single number conflates locating from composing, imposes a binary cliff on a smooth S-curve, and ignores the lost-in-the-middle positional structure -- and both replace it with curves plus declared operating points, so the decision turns on the finer design choices. B is stronger on three of them. First, the separation mechanism: A isolates reasoning by physically placing all facts in a short 2K salient block, which is clean but structurally cannot tell you whether the model can reason four hops over a 200K document, the question a practitioner actually has; B measures reasoning at every context length and instead imposes a retrievability gate -- probe each of the N spans individually first, admit the item to the reasoning curve only if the spans were retrievable, and report the excluded items separately as retrieval failures. That preserves the length interaction while still attributing failures correctly, and it is the sharpest single idea in either response. Second, threshold semantics: B defines retention relative to each model's own short-context ceiling rather than an absolute floor, which is the right call for cross-model comparison since a model with an 82 percent baseline and one with 99 percent are otherwise incomparable, and it adds a half-life as a worst-case bound. Third, B decomposes reasoning into two independent variables -- fact count N and step count S -- correctly noting they stress different bottlenecks, whereas A collapses both into a single hop-depth d; and B's compositional algebra (product over per-span retrieval probabilities times the conditional reasoning term) is a usable predictive model, where A offers only the min as a loose upper bound. A has real counter-strengths that keep this close: taking the minimum over needle positions rather than the mean is the more operationally honest summary, the knee/inflection point is a genuinely better comparator than a threshold crossing, the failure-step distribution is a diagnostic B lacks, and A alone insists the threshold be pre-registered to prevent post-hoc cherry-picking. On balance B's confound control, comparability-robust thresholds and compositional algebra outweigh these."}

{"choice": "A", "rationale": "These are close: both open with the right scepticism (0.8 percent at p=0.03 is a hypothesis, not a conclusion), both demand the pre-registration document, the confidence interval rather than the bare p-value, the daily lift trajectory to separate novelty from steady state, segment breakdowns with intervals, guardrails including diversity and retention, and both land on a phased rollout with a long-term holdout. It leads with the sample-ratio-mismatch check -- raw counts, chi-squared, day-by-day count plot, treated as automatic invalidation -- which is the single most standard trustworthiness gate in experiment review and which B never mentions at all.
